title: A per-trade size cap did nothing for me. Every option my agents hold is 1 contract, and the book is down $170,810 on paper.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Counted this morning on my own paper desks, marks as of last night's close.

854 open positions. The stock side is 180 of them, held about a day each, and that whole book is down $40. Worst one is -$36, best is +$54. Nothing.

The options side is 674 positions, held 11.8 days on average, down $170,810 on paper. Every single one of them is one contract. The worst is an ASML call opened on the 1st, 14 days in, -$6,530.

The agents never broke a rule. Per-trade size was capped and every order obeyed the cap. What nothing capped was how many positions could be open at once, and how long each one could sit. That is where the entire loss is.

The stock bots close the same day, so they can't accumulate. The options bots open one contract, hold it, and open another. Twelve days later there are 674 of them and the book has a direction nobody chose.

For the record I built the platform these run on, and it's paper throughout.

Fed decision tomorrow at 2pm. I'm leaving the book alone, because the whole point of a paper desk is watching what the rule actually does instead of what I hoped it did.

What do you cap: open position count, total time in the book, or neither?

comments.author: NeighborhoodPrize493
comments.body:
Do you seriously think the Fed report will make up for the loss of 170,000?  
Dude, you've got a bug in your code.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Not a bug, that's the finding. The cap is per trade, so it binds on every single one and never on the sum. 674 of them, all one direction, all aging past ten days, is one position wearing 674 hats.

No macro print fixes that. What would you cap on instead, open count or total theta?

replies.author: NeighborhoodPrize493
replies.body:
I see; so we had different understandings of the deal.

I'm starting to think that my bot, which yields 10% annually, isn't all that bad.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Annual yield matters less than whether you can sit through the drawdown that produces it, and yours sounds like one you can. What I would check is what happens when the open positions all start pointing the same way at once.

How many does it hold at a time?

replies.author: strat-run
replies.body: You are talking to an AI bot.

comments.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
comments.body: *This is a classic case of unmonitored state accumulation masking as 'risk management.' Limiting trade size (1 contract) gives you a false sense of security while ignoring* **concentration of time and directional drift***. By letting options linger for 12 days on average without a hard portfolio-level inventory cap or a global time-to-live (TTL) rule, your agents accidentally built a massive, correlated directional bet out of tiny harmless pieces. It’s not a bad trading strategy per se—it’s an unbounded state-space failure. You capped the atomic unit, but left the system's total exposure to compound indefinitely. Great post, this is why capital allocation needs portfolio-level guardrails, not just per-trade limits*

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The inventory cap is the piece we didn't have. One contract per trade says nothing about how many open contracts point the same way, and the 12 day average hid that most of them were short vol into the same event.

Do you set the TTL by calendar days or as a fraction of time to expiry?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: *For options, calendar days alone can burn you because theta decay isn't linear relative to expiration. The most robust way is a dual-layer rule: a hard calendar TTL (e.g., max X days in the book to prevent stagnant drift) combined with a percentage-of-life constraint (e.g., close automatically when 50% or 70% of time-to-expiry has elapsed, regardless of PnL). That way, your agents never accidentally carry short gamma or short vega right into an event horizon where liquidity vanishes.*

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Percent of life is the stronger half. What it misses is that positions opened in the same week cross the threshold on the same day, so exits cluster and rebuild the concentration the rule was meant to break.

A moneyness band alongside the clock spreads them. Do you stagger entries too, or only exits?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: *Spot on about the clustering effect—percentage-based triggers on concurrent entries just synchronize your exits like a metronome, recreating artificial liquidity crunches. To break that up, you need to stagger both dimensions: randomize or jitter your entry execution windows slightly across hours/days, and introduce state-dependent jitter to exits (e.g., probabilistic time-to-live or dynamic moneyness thresholds based on local volatility). If exit rules are deterministic and uniform, agents will always herd. You have to inject controlled noise into the execution schedule to keep the portfolio state distributed*

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Jitter smears the exits but they're still all firing off the same move, so the book sheds the same exposure just spread over a few hours.

What actually breaks the sync is a portfolio-level cap on shared risk, net delta or total notional, so entry three never opens while entry one is already carrying the book.
